title: The Cream-Ware Invoice That Reported Wedgwood's Amputation
dek: In May 1768, with his new factory still being built, Josiah Wedgwood had his painful right leg amputated without anaesthetic, and within weeks was writing that the unanswered letters were slowing his recovery.

story.event: Having his right leg amputated while the Etruria works were being built
story.summary: On 28 May 1768, while his Etruria factory was being built and his partnership with Thomas Bentley was about to begin, the potter Josiah Wedgwood had his right leg amputated at home in Burslem without anaesthetic, after years of pain in a knee weakened by childhood smallpox. His infant son Richard died within the week; his wife Sarah dressed the wound and handled his letters, and by late June he was visiting his works. Etruria opened on 13 June 1769.
paragraphs: On Saturday 28 May 1768, Peter Swift, the accountant at Josiah Wedgwood's pottery in Burslem, wrote out an invoice of cream ware for the London warehouse and added a note at the foot. His master, he wrote, had that day had his leg taken off and was "as well as can be expected after such an execution."

Wedgwood was by then potter to Queen Charlotte, and his cream-coloured earthenware was sold as Queen's ware. His new factory, Etruria, was rising beside the planned Trent and Mersey Canal, and his Liverpool friend Thomas Bentley had agreed to be his partner. His right knee had been weak since smallpox in boyhood. In April 1768 he wrote that he had "over walk'd & over work'd" it. His surgeon, Mr Bent of Newcastle-under-Lyme, gave him an emetic, and Wedgwood later described what followed: when the pain left the knee he grew hot and short of breath, and was glad to feel it return.

A second surgeon was called in and amputation was agreed. His Victorian biographer Eliza Meteyard wrote that Wedgwood proposed it himself, having resolved to lose the leg before Etruria opened. There was no anaesthetic. By his biographers' accounts Bentley was with him, and Wedgwood would not have the operation hidden from his view. Within the week his son Richard, about ten months old, died after an illness of the bowels. Sarah Wedgwood, who had been nursing the child, dressed her husband's wound, wrote his letters and kept business away from him.

On 13 June he added a postscript to a letter Bentley had written for him: it was the first time he had "set pen to paper, except to sign my name, since the Surgeons laid their hands on me." About a month after the operation he told Bentley he had "turned my surgeon adrift, and Sally and I are sole managers now," but admitted that the pile of unanswered letters "confines me to the house, and retards my perfect recovery." Sarah, he added, was ordering him to give over. By late June he was visiting his works; he walked on wooden legs for the rest of his life. When Etruria opened on 13 June 1769, Wedgwood threw its first six vases while Bentley turned the wheel.

quote.text: For this also is a part of life, like walking, like sailing, like journeying by land, so also is fever. Do you read when you are walking? No. Nor do you when you have a fever.
quote.locator: Discourses, Book III, Chapter X, "In what manner we ought to bear sickness"
quote.source_title: A Selection from the Discourses of Epictetus with the Encheiridion, tr. George Long, Project Gutenberg eBook #10661
quote.connection: Within weeks of the operation Wedgwood was answering letters and admitting they slowed his healing. Epictetus treats illness as a part of life with its own proper work, as walking is, and nobody reads while walking. Sarah, ordering her husband to give over, seems to have taken the philosopher's side.

reflection: The courage in this story is the part that usually gets retold. The more useful detail is the one Wedgwood admitted himself: the unanswered letters were keeping him indoors and slowing the healing. Work does not stop arriving because a body needs mending, and the pile has a way of making the mending take longer.

Epictetus does not ask you to be brave about being unwell. He asks you to let being unwell be the day's task, the way walking is the task while you walk. Colleagues, family and the work all write to you. Wedgwood had someone at his side telling him to stop. On some days the right reply to everyone is a later one.
invitation: Pick one unanswered message that has been sitting on your mind, and decide on purpose that it will wait until you have rested. Write down the day you will answer it, and then leave it alone.

sources.title: The Life of Josiah Wedgwood, from his private correspondence and family papers, volume II (1866)
sources.publisher: Eliza Meteyard (Hurst and Blackett); scan at the Internet Archive
sources.supports: Wedgwood's letter to William Cox of 30 April 1768 about having over-walked and over-worked his leg; Mr Bent of Newcastle ordering an emetic; Wedgwood's own account of the pain leaving the knee and the heat and difficulty of breathing that followed; a second surgeon called and amputation agreed, suggested by Wedgwood himself, who had resolved to have the leg removed before opening Etruria (as told by Wedgwood to Mrs Mayer of Newcastle); amputation on 28 May 1768 with two surgeons and Bentley present; Wedgwood refusing to have the operation hidden from his view; Peter Swift's note appended to an invoice of cream ware ('piggins, cream pots, salts'); Swift's later note that 'Master Dicky' (Richard, about ten months old) had died after a complaint in his bowels; Sarah dressing the wound, giving his medicines and writing his letters; the 13 June 1768 postscript ('the first time I have set pen to paper, except to sign my name, since the Surgeons laid their hands on me'); the 20 June letter about two airings in a chaise and leaving off laudanum; the later letter about turning the surgeon adrift and Sally ordering him to give over; visiting Etruria by the end of June; Wedgwood's 1770 reference to 'St Amputation Day' on 31 May.

sources.title: Josiah Wedgwood, F.R.S.: His Personal History (1897 edition)
sources.publisher: Samuel Smiles (John Murray); Cornell University Library scan at the Internet Archive
sources.supports: Smallpox in boyhood and the lasting trouble with his knee; Wedgwood's letter to Cox about over-walking and over-working his leg and consulting Mr Bent; amputation on 28 May 1768 by Mr Bent assisted by a local surgeon, with no anaesthetic; Bentley coming over from Liverpool; Wedgwood watching the surgeons; Sarah conducting his correspondence and dressing the wound while attending their dying son; Peter Swift's note 'as well as can be expected after such an execution'; the letter about a month later saying the backlog of replies 'confines me to the house, and retards my perfect recovery' and 'I have turned my surgeon adrift, and Sally and I are sole managers now'; wooden legs; Etruria's ornamental works opening on 13 June 1769 with Wedgwood throwing vases while Bentley turned the wheel.

sources.title: Wedgwood, Josiah (1730–1795), by Robin Reilly, Oxford Dictionary of National Biography (2004), as reproduced on a Wedgwood family history blog
sources.publisher: Oxford University Press (text reproduced at wedgwoodfamily.blogspot.com, March 2009)
sources.supports: Smallpox leaving his right knee permanently weakened and unable to work the kick-wheel unaided; the 1765 commission from Queen Charlotte and the renaming of his creamware as Queen's ware in 1766; purchase of the Ridgehouse estate in 1766 and Etruria's position on the projected Trent and Mersey Canal; Bentley's agreement in February 1767 to become his partner in ornamental wares; 'over walk'd & over work'd' (Wedgwood MS 17760, 30 April 1768); amputation four weeks later, without anaesthetic, in his own house; by the third week of June visiting his Burslem factory and the Etruria site; wooden legs for the rest of his life; Etruria inaugurated on 13 June 1769 with six 'First Day's Vases' thrown by Wedgwood on a wheel turned by Bentley; Sarah's dowry of about £4000; Richard living less than a year; birth probably on 12 July 1730.

sources.title: Don't tread on me (review of Tristram Hunt, The Radical Potter)
sources.publisher: London Review of Books, Vol. 44 No. 24 (Brigid von Preussen, 15 December 2022)
sources.supports: The accountant's note to the London office that Wedgwood had had his leg taken off and was 'as well as can be expected after such an execution'; amputation without anaesthetic in 1768 after decades of pain from childhood smallpox; his infant son Richard dying a few days after the surgery; orders and invoices continuing to pile up; wooden prosthetics; creamware called Queensware after Queen Charlotte's order.

sources.title: Did you know? Josiah Wedgwood's leg
sources.supports: Right leg amputated on 28 May 1768, with no anaesthetics or antiseptics; childhood smallpox as the likely root of the knee disease, with Jewitt's dissent; a rapid recovery; a wooden leg made by Mr Addison of Long Acre.

cross_checks.claim: Wedgwood's right leg was amputated on 28 May 1768, without anaesthetic.
The amputation followed an April 1768 strain of his weak right knee and took place about four weeks later at his home.
A works clerk reported the operation to the London office on the day, writing that Wedgwood was as well as could be expected after such an execution.
His infant son Richard died within days of the operation.
By late June 1768 Wedgwood was well enough to visit his works and the Etruria site.
Etruria opened on 13 June 1769, with Wedgwood throwing the first vases while Bentley turned the wheel.
His creamware became Queen's ware after Queen Charlotte's patronage.

research_notes: No outcome figures are central here, but several details disagree. Age: the LRB and the Spectator (both reviewing Tristram Hunt) say he was 38; the ODNB gives his probable birth date as 12 July 1730, which makes him 37 on 28 May 1768, so the story gives no age. Date: Peter Swift's invoice note is dated 28 May 1768 and all sources use that day; Meteyard notes that Wedgwood himself wrote of 'St Amputation Day' on 31 May 1770, and Smiles wrongly says the leg was amputated on 'the eighth', so the story uses the contemporary invoice. Surgeons: the ODNB says 'a local surgeon'; Smiles says Mr Bent assisted by a local surgeon; Meteyard says two surgeons, and Swift's second note refers to 'both the Surgeons'. The story names Bent and says a second surgeon was called. Bentley's presence: Smiles states it; Meteyard says it is 'evident' from the letters; the LRB is silent, so the story attributes it to his biographers. The claim that Wedgwood proposed the amputation and had resolved on it before Etruria opened comes from Meteyard, who says Mrs Mayer of Newcastle had it from Wedgwood personally; the story attributes it to Meteyard. Cause: the ODNB ties the weak knee to smallpox (c.1745-46) and records a 1762 fall in Liverpool and the April 1768 strain; the Spectator review says the amputation followed 'complications after a carriage accident', and Jewitt (quoted by thepotteries.org) also blamed an accident; the story sticks to the documented knee history and does not assign a single cause. Where the leg was cut (above or below the knee) differs even within thepotteries.org, so the story leaves it out. Smallpox age varies (11 in Smiles, about 12 in Hunt, c.1745-46 in the ODNB); the story says 'in boyhood'. Richard's death: Swift's note written about seven days after the operation says he died 'on Thursday morning', which was 2 June 1768; the story says 'within the week'. Founder quotations are taken from Meteyard (13 June postscript), Smiles (the letter about a month after the operation, in Smiles's modernised spelling) and the ODNB (the April 1768 phrase). Funding: Wedgwood financed the works from trade and family money, including Sarah's dowry, said by the ODNB to be about £4000; there were no outside investors, so 'bootstrapped' is kept. The ODNB is cited from a family-history blog's reproduction because oxforddnb.com requires a subscription; Britannica and the Science Museum Group pages returned 403. The Epictetus passage comes from the discourse on bearing sickness, which goes on to say a sick man should not flatter or fear his physician.
